label: Sophomore Lounge
description: A sprawling seven-song double LP of conversational barfly rock, Davis half-sings dense, punning verses over a loose Roadhouse Band arrangement that folds pedal steel and violin into synths and programmed beats. It is dark, funny and grand at once, with guest harmonies from Will Oldham, Catherine Irwin and Lou Turner deepening its Drag City-indebted, David Berman-adjacent lineage. For listeners who want the modern high-water mark of wordy, tragicomic songwriting.
lineage: Davis fronted the earlier Louisville band State Champion before going solo with the Roadhouse Band; the record extends the Silver Jews/David Berman line of deadpan storytelling into the 2020s.

label: Sophomore Lounge
description: Davis's first billed Roadhouse Band record: a double-LP set of long, expansive songs that mix folk-rooted wordplay with synth textures, organ swells and pedal steel. The mood is melancholic and gentle rather than rowdy. A good entry point for the barfly-poet strain of the scene before New Threats from the Soul refined it further.
lineage: Follows Davis's work fronting State Champion; sounds indebted to Souled American, David Berman and Neil Young.

label: Sophomore Lounge
description: Ryan Davis's main band before his Roadhouse records: loose, twangy full-band arrangements built to carry his dense, surrealist wordplay. Send Flowers is their most fully realized record, with fiddle and ragged guitars under long, funny-sad verses. It sounds like a missing link between Silver Jews and the current Louisville deadpan-songwriter scene.
lineage: Direct predecessor to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band through Davis himself; sounds rooted in the Drag City deadpan lineage.

label: Sophomore Lounge
description: A punked-up country record steeped in Louisville's weird, unassuming rock scene, with fiddle and banjo scrapping against fuzzy guitars behind Ryan Davis's character sketches of postmasters, coroners and drinkers. It sounds close to Souled American and Palace Brothers, rough and funny.
lineage: Early-period State Champion, before Davis's Roadhouse Band turn; sounds indebted to the Drag City/Palace lineage that runs to Silver Jews and Purple Mountains.

label: Wharf Cat Records
description: Poole's third solo LP pairs his golden, deadpan baritone with a live band plus old-school synthesizers, widening his millennial-malaise persona into songs about mortality and time rather than just dead-end jobs. The title track, named for the Mac beachball icon, is eerie and gently funny.
lineage: Poole's country songwriting sounds descended from Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson filtered through Brooklyn's DIY scene; the drum-machine-plus-pedal-steel sound recalls Silver Jews.

label: Wharf Cat Records
description: Poole's second LP graduates from bedroom drum-machine country to a full honky-tonk band with wailing pedal steel. It updates classic countrypolitan storytelling for a young, broke, romantically alienated urban narrator, sung in his dry baritone.
lineage: Follows his debut Wideass Highway; sounds like Haggard/Nelson/Kristofferson-style storytelling country moved into an ironic, digital-age idiom.

label: Self-released
description: Poole's self-released debut, a bedroom-recorded set built from drum machines and synthesizers under twangy vocal melodies, already showing the wry, deadpan lyric style he'd sharpen on later records. Rougher and more lo-fi than what followed, it is a deep cut for fans who want the beginning of the story.
lineage: The starting point for Poole's country-by-way-of-DIY-indie sound that would develop through The Freelancer's Blues and The Rainbow Wheel of Death.
key_tracks: Don't You Think I'm Funny Anymore?

label: Mtn Laurel Recording Co.
description: A bittersweet, sharpened set of folk-rock songs full of shared-memory and loss storytelling drawn from his Asheville circle. Miller's plainspoken, half-sung delivery and homespun production put the focus on the writing over any studio polish.
lineage: Follows Miller's debut Haw Creek; sounds of a piece with the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

label: Ruination Records
description: Miller's debut full-length: hushed, homespun songwriting set against tape-hiss production and found-sound experiments. Pump organ, dulcimer-like textures and quiet guitar give it a front-porch, family-archive feel.
lineage: Predates Losin'; sounds close to the Asheville scene around MJ Lenderman and Wednesday.

label: Sub Pop
description: The former Pearls and Brass drummer's third album drapes his cavernous, deadpan baritone over sampled loops and drum machines rather than a bar band. Its storytelling core of plainspoken, dark, small-town character studies fits the same funny-sad lineage as his songwriting peers.
lineage: Follows All Hell (2012) and Me Moan (2013), both pre-2014 and outside this lane's window; Carnation extends his baritone-narrator style into a more electronic production.
borderline_note: All Hell (2012) and Me Moan (2013) are pre-2014 and fall outside the C2 era window; not included.

label: Self-released
description: Gibson's fourth full-length, a slow-building record of Florida noir vignettes that trades his earlier sample-collage approach for a more spacious, bar-at-closing-time mood. His deep, deadpan baritone carries Southern gothic storytelling over sparse arrangements.
lineage: Fourth Daughn Gibson LP, following Carnation (2015); continues his deadpan-narrator persona in a stripped-down mode.

label: Self-released
description: The ex-Ona keyboardist's debut swaps that band's rock for piano-man virtuosity and Zevon-ish snark. It is funny without playing as a comedy record, closer to plainspoken confession set to rolling piano.
lineage: Follows Goodall's time in Ona; sounds indebted to the Randy Newman/Warren Zevon line of wry piano storytelling.

label: Self-released
description: A piano-driven, introspective record about returning to his West Virginia hometown, with the sophisticated melodic sense of Made In America turned toward homesickness rather than jokes. It rounds out Goodall's small catalog of plainspoken, piano-led songwriting.
lineage: Follows Made In America and a Levon Helm Studios live set; continues his piano-based storytelling, which sounds indebted to Zevon and Newman.

label: Self-released
description: A live set cut at Levon Helm Studios, revisiting Made In America highlights in a stripped, in-the-room performance. Goodall's rolling piano and wry vocals come across warm and direct, with the room sound left in.
lineage: Live companion to Made In America, recorded shortly after that LP's release.

label: Mama Bird Recording Co.
description: Smart, unfussy, mildly twangy folk built around dry, plainspoken wit about small-town Montana life. It sounds as gentle as Bahamas or Andy Shauf, but the lyrics carry the same funny-sad economy as his barroom-storyteller peers.
lineage: Missoula, Montana songwriter whose work sits at the folk/country-adjacent end of the deadpan-storyteller lineage.

label: Self-released
description: A keys-heavy, conversational sophomore album about relationships, mixing fingerpicked folk, indie rock and pop confessionals. The Yiddish title signals the same rueful, self-deprecating humor that runs through his songwriting.
lineage: Follows Halper's 2020 debut Alrightnik; a Nashville songwriter working the same wry, wordy vein as his singer-songwriter peers.

label: Self-released
description: Halper's debut mixes wry self-reflection with intricate fingerpicked instrumentals. Its title, Yiddish slang for a crass nouveau-riche success story, sets up the self-deprecating tone he'd carry into Schlemiel.
lineage: Debut predecessor to Schlemiel; sounds indebted to Elliott Smith and fingerstyle players like Leo Kottke and William Tyler.

label: Sophomore Lounge
description: Three Nashville songwriters trading instruments and lead vocals on an easygoing patio album with shaggy-dog charm. Feelies-ish jangle and Little Feat-style tempo shifts run through their group songwriting.
lineage: Sounds close to the Nashville dive-bar scene of Lambchop and Silver Jews, and to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band.

label: Self-released
description: The trio's follow-up to Real Time leans further into playful genre-hopping, with lounge, B-52's pulse and Glen Campbell dust. It keeps the same trading-instruments, trading-verses songwriting method.
lineage: Sounds close to Ryan Davis & the Roadhouse Band and MJ Lenderman and the Wind.

album: I'm Sad as Hell and I'm Not Going to Fake It Anymore
label: Sipsman
description: Janky, livewire guitars and winking humor meet surprisingly massive choruses, somewhere between Amen Dunes and a Lou Reed doing country. The title alone sets the funny-sad tone that carries through songs about content-creation anxiety and modern malaise.
lineage: Sounds close to the Northeast indie-twang of Greg Freeman and Lily Seabird; extends jokey, confessional indie-folk songwriting into anthemic rock territory.

label: Self-released
description: London songwriter Michael Rea's charming, conversational folk-rock record moves at an ambling, unhurried pace, its plainspoken verses and breezy melodies squarely in the wordy funny-sad tradition despite its UK setting.
lineage: A non-US example of the Prine/Berman deadpan-storyteller mode, showing the style's reach beyond its American scenes.
borderline_note: Non-US (London) artist; included on style/sound fit per lane definition, not scene.

label: Black Mountain // Soundly Music
description: Bradshaw's character-driven songwriting captures life split between the north Georgia mountains and the touring road, recorded in five live days at Fellowship Hall Sound. Reviewers place him alongside Jason Isbell for narrative-driven, plainspoken Southern songwriting shot through with dry humor.
lineage: Follows his 2021 LP Calico Jim, cut at the same Little Rock studio; part of a loose north-Georgia Appalachian storytelling trilogy completed by Thus Spoke the Fool.

label: Black Mountain Music / Soundly Music
description: Bradshaw's character-driven historical songwriting, humanizing north-Georgia history and working-class locals. His rough, drawled voice sits over sparse, Appalachian-rooted arrangements.
lineage: Follows Calico Jim and North Georgia Rounder in his run of north-Georgia story records.

label: Memorials of Distinction / Dog Day Records
description: The Oakland quartet's breezy, affecting debut LP, with four singers and songwriters trading lead vocals from laconic to full-throated. Conversational lyrics and a living-room-session intimacy carry its funny-sad, plainspoken storytelling.
lineage: Sounds of a piece with the funny-sad, plainspoken songwriting in the barroom-storyteller lane.

label: Memorials of Distinction / Dog Day Records
description: Mildred's debut EP introduces the four-singer, four-songwriter format they'd expand on Fenceline. It is homemade and intimate, with trading lead vocals over living-room-scale guitar arrangements.
lineage: Precedes Fenceline as the band's first release.

label: ATO Records
description: Fritz folds synths and drum samples into his unconventional, wisecracking country songwriting, moving past the straighter honky-tonk of Dad Country toward a more hopeful, idiosyncratic sound. Titles like 'Chihuahua Rescue' signal the deadpan comic streak underneath.
lineage: Follows Dad Country (2013); as Jonny Corndawg-turned-Fritz's later work, it sits at the more experimental, funny-sad end of the outlaw-adjacent Nashville scene.
borderline_note: Earlier Fritz records (as Jonny Corndawg / Dad Country era) are placed in V6 per seed note; Sweet Creep and Debbie Downers are logged here as his later, more idiosyncratic work.

label: Gar Hole Records
description: Fritz's return after a long break turns blue-collar everyday life into wry, anthemic country songs. Honky-tonk band arrangements back his nasal, joke-laced delivery, with the humor always edging toward sadness.
lineage: Follows Sweet Creep (2016) after a near-decade recording gap; continues his idiosyncratic, joke-laced country songwriting.

label: Self-released
description: A cellist-songwriter's wry, meticulously detailed record, pairing relaxed, lush chamber-pop arrangements (cello interludes throughout) with DIY-punk detours and dryly funny lyrics. Closer to bedroom chamber-folk than a bar band, but its joke-then-gut-punch songwriting places it near the deadpan storyteller lineage.
lineage: A borderline Core inclusion: less bar-band than her C2 peers, but shares the funny-sad lyrical mode with Prine/Berman-style songwriters.
borderline_note: Borderline C2 fit: cello-based chamber pop rather than bar-band arrangement; included per seed note and Terry coverage, could also read as Context/indie-folk adjacent.
